Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate those three questions. First, on the question of the advisory process, some very serious allegations have been made. What we did initially under the leadership of the Speaker of the House when he was Minister of Fisheries and Oceans was to create a policy advisory group on the Atlantic Coast called the Atlantic Regional Council or ARC. 1 can assure the Hon. Member that on that council sit people who carry, for the most part, no political affiliation, and those who might, carry affiliations of all three political parties.
We had a problem with the equivalent of PARC, which was not a policy group, but more a management advisory group. Eighteen of the 20 positions were held by representatives of the commercial fishery, that is, fishermen. However, the native sector had abandoned the organization as did, in the latter stages, the recreational fishing representation. It was then totally inappropriate to give proper representation to all of the the important policy issues on which I, as Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, required advice.
We created a PARC on the West Coast, not a national PARC although we commend that decision as well, but a Pacific Area Regional Council, the equivalent of ARC, which consists of 12 members and a chairperson, thirteen in total, appointed to be my principle source of advice on policy issues, and appointed to represent people who are respected for their eminent stature and knowledge in various parts of the fishery, commercial, native, recreational and general interest, as well as the business aspect. Those selections were based on advice to me from many organizations, notwithstanding the fact that the United Fishery and Allied Workers Union refused to offer a nominee, and notwithstanding the fact that the large seine boat sector declined an invitation. Those are matters I expect to adjust in future.
Supply
On my Pacific Area Regional Council, again there would not be very many of those 13 individuals who would have a political affiliation, but of those who do would be representative of all three political parties. I could not live with a council where the members were changing and always had to report back to their organizations to call a special meeting to obtain the organization's consent, and to have a system of voting where some groups who could not have it their way had to leave because their views were always vetoed. I have a created a consensus group of advisory people, much as the federal Cabinet or a political caucus operates. They do not advise me when they do not come to me with consensus. That is what I seek and that is why this new advisory structure is so important to the future of the Pacific coast fishery.
In regard to the point the Hon. Member implies about the Prime Minister appointing a Minister, I was appointed two years ago this week as Minister of Fisheries and Oceans for Canada. I give my undivided attention and devotion to these duties and have the full support of the Prime Minister to that effect. No one has been appointed to speak for me, notwithstanding the fact that from time to time in the House Acting Ministers are designated when Ministers cannot be in the House. I do not even know what the Hon. Member is implying. It seems to be something mischievous or scurrilous. I fully carry out all of my duties as the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans for all Canada.
Finally, I can assure the Hon. Member that the objective of the Canada-U.S. trade agreement is to find means, by the reduction and elimination of tariffs and the unbiased application of U.S. trade remedy laws, to gain more added value, more investment and employment opportunities in the fishery of Canada. Anything that operates to the detriment of that will be opposed by this Government and is clearly protected against in the Canada-U.S. trade agreement, notwithstanding the GATT panel recommendation to which the Hon. Member referred.
My colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade, who will speak later, will elaborate on this. Many GATT countries use measures which are accepted under the GATT and consistent with the obligations of those countries under the GATT to ensure that supply of raw materials, in this case fish, is available on a priority basis to serve the needs of established plants and industries in their countries. We expect to enjoy the same privilege all the other members of GATT have in that respect.

I certainly do appreciate the clarification, Mr. Speaker, but the comment still stands. Hopefully, when we are dealing with fisheries issues in this House the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans will in fact be the person who responds and who is in fact held accountable for that extremely important area. With his assurance, I will carefully watch in the future how this matter unfolds.
I would like to follow on with some of the unfortunate aspects of the Minister's speech. With respect to the nature of the partisanship in this Government, to which I had alluded, in the appointment of the Pacific Area Regional Council, we have now seen a politicization of the advice process. The previous Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the individual who has distinguished himself as a very competent and respected Speaker in the House of Commons, was in fact a very respected Minister of Fisheries. The Minister was open, very knowledgeable and concerned about environmental matters. He was concerned with all matters and aspects of the fishery. Had that Minister continued in the role of appointing the advisory committee we may have seen the direction continue in that the advice and the advisory committee itself would not be politicized. The individuals who have to live with the results of that advice and the management plans that are put into place would not feel that they had been exploited politically and that the management plan had come about as a result of partisan advice.
1 do not say that with malicious intent. It is my hope that it will be recognized and that the difficulties that are being created in the fishing community as a result of people's feelings in that direction can be rectified as the advisory committee grows and develops. I hope that it will not be stunted as it is today. I hope that criticisms against it will be examined and that improvements will be made to it so that there can be growing confidence with respect to the types of decisions that come out of it.
It is also my hope that as of the day after the next election every member of the advisory committee will not be fired and a whole new partisan group of individuals appointed to give political advice on management programs. Personally, I see that as a very dangerous trend. I know that many people in the west coast fisheries also see that as a very serious trend. I think it can be rectified quickly.
The Minister also alluded to the two approaches to an advisory committee. Of course, the dilemma is that to bring about some kind of consensus, or at least widespread support for management programs, is something which will never be. Dissension will always be there because of the underlying principle involved, that there are not enough fish and it is the fault of the Tories. Prior to 1984 there were not enough fish and it was the fault of the Liberals. Those fish were always being misallocated. One group was always getting a better deal than the other. Even when the NDP forms the Government those problems will not leave us.
What I think has to happen in this particular situation is that the advisory groups must represent the major players in the fisheries. If a major player group is involved in the fisheries and has no say on that committee, or at least no effective say, then it will not be content with the management results that come from it. When major players are eliminated the entire Government and the Parliament of Canada will be a target for constant and ongoing criticism with respect to what is going on. That is not in the interest of anyone. The people who are on the committee must enjoy the confidence of the group they represent.
The other option is the one which has been chosen by the Minister. The previous Government chose this approach as well, although it was a bit more careful to ensure broader representation. It had the wise person approach to the committee. What is done is that individuals who are not accountable to organizations but who have broad knowledge of the industry and certain aspects of it are selected. Or, perhaps, they have broad knowledge of the economy of the west coast fishery, let us say. I have been told that a wise Tory is a contradiction in terms. But giving the benefit of the doubt in this particular case, there are a number of wise individuals who have been appointed to this committee.
Unfortunately, in selecting individuals who are not accountable to organizations we end up with a situation in which people think that they were selected on the basis of their political affiliation and their partisan view. I see that the Minister is shaking his head. It is possible that I might be incorrect. I live a very sheltered life on the coast of British Columbia. I am not widely known as a partisan individual. What we have to see is a very responsive move by the federal Government with respect to the issue of land claims. In British Columbia, many fishermen are suggesting that the federal Government is driving a wedge between the native people and the fishermen to provoke conflict. It has been suggested that in the political management of the fisheries it is in the Government's interest to have various sectors of the industry fighting with each other. What happens is that the federal Government correctly begins to negotiate with the native people on the coast of British Columbia about their access and rights to fishing. Then it actively supports the defence leagues against the Indian fishery to become involved in advertising programs and, basically, to inflame this discussion, thus moving it to an almost racial conflict.
What has happened is that we do have a full-blown conflict between native people and a number of fishermen on the coast of British Columbia. Other voices are saying that what is at fault here, and what has created problems in the fishing industry, is the Government in its desire to divide and rule. It is dividing those who are natural allies, those who should be working together in the industry. It is doing so in a provocative and, in my opinion, dangerous manner.
What should be happening is that the Government should be moving on a broad based settlement of native land claims. Fishermen are asking that that happen. They do not want to see fish as the only currency of settlement of claim, or as the interim settlement of claim. They want to see a fair deal for the native people. They do not want to see what happened on Lyell Island happen again. Nor do they want to see what happened on Meares Island or in the Stein Valley of British Columbia happen again. It is being said that the Social Credit Government in Victoria and, indeed, the federal Government in Ottawa in working together are actually driving wedges between native people and loggers, native people and fishermen, in order to start community conflicts instead of getting people to work together. In the fishing industry it is critical. There is clear evidence that the federal Government has been supporting both sides of the issue. It can only be doing that in the same way as the classic 20th century arms merchant who makes money by selling guns to both sides in a war. This is totally unacceptable.

That is what we are talking about now. That is the fleet that the people in St. Pierre and Miquelon detest. That is the fleet over which they call public meetings. They say that they must do something against the Government of France because the Government of Canada lacks the political will, as the Hon. Member who presented this motion said, to do anything about it.

There has been the complete opposite of inept management. There has been "ept" management. One would think that Jake was in the Minister's position. Let me give one or two examples of "ept" management.
We are getting effective enforcement of the 200-mile limit that went into effect in 1977. That "ept" and effective management began with this Minister who has improved in every direction the enforcement of the 200-mile limit. He has placed observers on all foreign trawlers who fish within those limits. He has placed observers on domestic trawlers who fish in 2J3KL for the first three months of each year. Even our domestic trawlers have observers. Why? To help protect inshore fishermen.

We also had the increasing of fines for illegal fishing in the 200-mile limit. I do not know how much they have increased. They have quadrupled or quintupled up to $500,000 an offence. The Minister says tenfold. Our patrol vessels have been armed. They are no longer afraid to meet naval tugs like the La Centure which has a machine gun on her stern. The French will find our patrol vessels now have a machine gun on their front end. This is because of the Minister.
The Minister has acquired a dual-engine helicopter for surveillance purposes. He has hired or contracted with Atlantic Airways for a new radar patrol facility for the 200-mile limit.
This resolution talks about inept management of Canada's fisheries. I am not even going to touch on the West Coast or central Canada or Lake Winnipegosis or any of those other lakes. I am not going to touch on the North. I am only going to touch on the east. This is the most "ept" management Canada has ever had in the fishery on the East Coast of Canada in the person of our friend here from British Columbia, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
1 will not go into other aspects of management because we do not have all that much time. The motion refers to lack of support for the inshore fishery. I gave one example of how the Minister is ensuring that stocks of fish are available for the inshore fishermen. All Members will know that over the last three or four years there has been some difficulty because the fish are not coming inshore in as great a number as in the past. In 1986, inshore fish landings in Newfoundland and Labrador amounted to 281.655 million tonnes, with a landed value of $135,365 million. That is for the inshore fishery alone.
This year, to the end of September, inshore landings have totalled 195.616 thousand tonnes, and the landed value of $149,248 million is already greater than the whole landed value of last year.
While the catch appears to be down, the year is not yet over, the value of the catch is up considerably. It does leave some problems of course for the fishermen who were not lucky enough to get any fish or very little. If necessary, programs will be introduced to help them, just as the Minister introduced a special program for inshore fishermen in the last three years who were in a bad position with respect to unemployment insurance.
Let me make one other point with respect to the inshore fishery. I want to mention the Minister's Small Craft Harbours Revitalization Program. That is a three-year $150 million inshore fishery program for major repairs and infrastructure over and above the ongoing A-base spending of the Minister's Department for operation and maintenance of $48.5 million a year. It is a tremendous program.

The third criticism raised by the Hon. Member is the lack of political will to assert Canada's rights in the Canada-France dispute. That is absolutely contrary to the facts. Since last

February particularly, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) and I, under the direction of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have handled this dispute firmly and I believe capably. While we always had good negotiators, we now have a first-class outside negotiator in the person of Mr. Fortier.
I do not have time to go into all the details of what we have done, but at the moment there is an impasse. We had meetings with France which ended on October 9. As an example of how firm we have been, in February we closed Canadian ports to French fishing vessels to show the French that we were not satisfied with their attitude and with their over-fishing in the disputed zone of 3PS. In March, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans closed Burgeo Banks so that the fishermen of St. Pierre and Miquelon cannot fish in Burgeo Banks.
In August, the Minister closed all other areas of 3PS, including the western gullies which are outside the disputed zone, to French fishing vessels.
We have placed reasonable offers before the French because we are worried about over-fishing in the disputed zone of 3PS and what effect that will have on Canadian and Newfoundland fishermen, particularly on the south coast of Newfoundland. On October 9, when the French broke off negotiations and asked us to go to arbitration, quoting us under Article 10 of the infamous Liberal treaty of 1972, we said that we are not going to arbitration on fishery quotas under the treaty. We said we would not go to arbitration on quotas at all, but only consider giving quotas if the French reduce their fishing in disputed area 3PS, and agree to go to arbitration on the boundaries of St. Pierre and Miquelon. We told France that they will receive no quotas in Canadian waters in 1988 under this undesirable and unsatisfactory treaty of 1972 unless they begin to bargain with us in a sensible and reasonable manner. We said there will be no quotas for France in Canadian waters in 1988 despite the treaty, which French actions have made unworkable. The lack of reasonableness of the Government of France in this negotiation has made this treaty unworkable. Since the French have made it unworkable, we do not intend to go to arbitration and allow anyone outside Canada to decide what quotas might be in Canadian waters, despite the wording of this infamous Liberal treaty of 1972. That is our position.
The French have agreed to resume negotiations on the compromise with respect to the boundary dispute. There was a meeting on November 6, dealing with these technical legal matters, and I believe another meeting will be held at the end of November.
We witnessed a disgusting spectacle from the NDP ranks last January and February. The Leader of the New Democratic Party called for Canada to go into battle and use the Navy to clear the French ships off the sea. We saw Rambo Jewett, Battleship Broadbent and Hotspur Harris-the former lambs of peace. They are all for peace in the NDP. Their motto normally is: "peace at any price", except in the Canada-France matter. They wanted to let slip the dogs of war.

What a pernicious load of piffle. What have the Americans done? They made a complaint. 1 have five minutes. That is great. I can handle this adequately, then.
The Americans made a complaint under the GATT. The GATT should be a magical name to the members of the Official Opposition and members of the New Democratic Party because they have been harkening about the GATT ever since we started discussing free trade arrangements with the United States, since the U.S.-Canada free trade discussions began. They said: "Oh, we would go multilateral". The Leader of the New Democratic Party is a multilateralist. He does not want anything to do with the United States where, unfortunately, 75 per cent or 78 per cent of all Canada's exports go. Mr. Broadbent does not want anything to do with the U.S. That is unimportant. He is a great multilateralist. He is sitting on a $2 billion investment from General Motors in Oshawa and he is so darned selfish that he does not want to share the benefits of that kind of thing with anyone else in Canada. That is Mr. Broadbent for you.
But they ail believe in the GATT. The Leader of the Official Opposition, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra, believes in the multilateral. Now, he is against free trade in connection with our agreement. He is for free trade, he is against this agreement, or he is against this agreement and he is for free trade. Anyway, he is for free trade but he is also against free trade. He is on both sides of the free trade issue, he is for and against everything. His mug is on one side, his wump is on the other, and he has not even been around all week anyway. That is where he is on free trade.
What is the alternative of the Official Opposition to our negotiations with the U.S. on free trade? It has no alternative except to mention GATT. Unfortunately, there was a GATT panel ruling the other day in connection with certain restrictions pertaining to the sale of unprocessed salmon and herring in British Columbia. We want that fish processed in Canada, naturally. There is a regulation which says it has to be processed in Canada. The U.S. challenged that, as is its
right-the right of any member of GATT to challenge anything they think is protective-and it managed to get a panel to agree with it. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) are battling that all the way. We do not know what the final outcome will be. But did you notice, Mr. Speaker, that as soon as there was a decision contrary to what we conceived to be our interests in the GATT, the lack of enthusiasm for GATT on the Liberal and New Democratic Party opposition side and the criticism we received from Mr. GATT Broadbent? GATT Broadbent got up and: "GATT, GATT, GATT, GATT, gittle". Do you remember Danny Kaye, Mr. Speaker? He used to go: gittle, gittle, gittle"? That was the Leader of the New Democratic Party.

They think they can fool the Canadian people, and now this resolution comes along and adds this piece of nonsense. We are fighting the case just as any Government here in Canada would fight the case. mineral resources? For four or five years it attempted to starve the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador in the struggle over who would control the ownership and management of the offshore resources. He has the gall to get up to suggest that we are taking some type of discriminatory steps against Ontario. Some 90 per cent of all of the exports of Ontario go to the United States of America. Of them a tremendous quantity move under the Auto Pact.
I am simply suggesting, and I will keep suggesting, and I will suggest it from one end of the country to the other in every community in Canada in which I speak, that if the sauce is good for the goose it is good for the gander. If a free trade auto pact arrangement is good for Ontario, then a free trade auto pact arrangement is good for the rest of Canada, and we are entitled to have it in the rest of Canada. That is what we will say. It is what we will keep saying. There is nothing discriminatory about that.
Where was the Hon. Member when his Party was discriminating against the West by placing a cap on what price it would be paid for its resources at a time when the resources were rising in value and when doing this was being done for the benefit of other parts of Canada? That is all part of being Canada. Sometimes one's area has to make a sacrifice for another area. So the Hon. Member should not wave his honourable finger at us saying that we should not use arguments about what part of Canada is benefiting from what.
We know that Ontario benefits from the Auto Pact. Can anyone deny that? I know that Newfoundland and Labrador do not derive any benefit whatsoever from the Auto Pact. But I know that Newfoundland and Labrador will derive a great deal of benefit from the free trade arrangement. Why? Because Newfoundland's exports are primarily resource-based.
The Hon. Member might be interested in this. The most important example of this in Newfoundland is the U.S. tariff structure for fish. The duty on processed seafood, including breaded, battered or value-added products averages 12 per cent. That is why in the past we have not been able to produce in Canada the higher value-added products. We have had to build plants behind the U.S. tariff wall in Boston and Gloucester to make fish fingers and all the breaded, battered and other value-added products. After the free trade arrangement goes into effect we will be able to do all of that value-added work here in Canada. The President of Fisheries Products International, Vic Young, said, "It means that our fish products-like the value-added products we produce at Burin, we would be able to put into the U.S. market without the existing tariff. We could thereby increase the amount of exports from the Newfoundland fishing industry. This would increase the number of jobs for Newfoundlanders. So what is good in terms of the Auto Pact is good in terms of the fishing industry. If there can be jobs in Ontario then we want to be in a position to have increased jobs in Newfoundland. We will not apologize for that.
The free trade agreement will ensure that there will be no new barriers to trade resulting from the abuse of technical standards. Our exports of fish through packaging requirements and through inspection regulations will not be able to be stopped. Our right to control foreign investment in the fishing industry will be maintained. All customs user fees on Canadian exports to the U.S., including fish, will be eliminated. The fishing industry will benefit from the dispute settlement mechanisms. I quote from Gordon Cummings of National Sea Products Ltd. who said:
The most important aspect to us was the dispute settlement mechanism and we got that. It's a hell of a gain for Canada ... As it stands now we cannot get fair treatment in the United States. The bi-national trade panel will bring a more sane approach from the United States. This is a straight win situation for
us.
He also predicted that National Sea would expand its workforce by 400 as exports to the U.S. increase. And the Hon. Member says he is against this free trade agreement. The Official Opposition says that it is against jobs and expanded jobs in the fishing industry of Canada. Members of the NDP say the same thing.
Finally, I just want to quote Carlyle. When someone wanted to introduce him to the poet Swinburne he said, "I have no desire to meet a person who if he sat in a sewer would add to it". That applies to some other people I could name.

Mr. Speaker, one rarely gets a chance in the House to enjoy a speech such as the one given by the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). Most of the day of a Member of Parliament is spent struggling with the complex problems of Canada and working into the late hours of the night. Rarely does one get the quality of stand-up comic that we have just been witness to in the House of Commons this afternoon. This hon. gentleman could stand and speak for hour after hour making humour and flashing cracks as quickly as he pleases with absolutely no content or relevance to the problem before us. it has been one of the most enjoyable and refreshing afternoons that I myself and many other people in the House have experienced in a long, long time. I now hope we can get back to business.
There is one matter about which I would like to ask the Hon. Member for St. John's West who is a former Minister of Justice. He had the responsibility of protecting the morals of Canadians. Perhaps he could explain this to the House. I understand that the residents of Dildo Hill have put the Minister of Fisheries through the beatification process and allowed sainthood to fall upon him. Is he taking any responsibility for stamping out the satanic cults that would have done that? That is the first question I would like to put to him since in this country the Minister is certainly viewed in many quarters as a representative of the forces of evil and the Conservative Government.
In the free trade situation again the conflicts between the two individuals are astounding. The Minister of Transport
November 20, 1987

(Mr. Crosbie), a prominent member of the Conservative Government is overriding the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) from British Columbia and saying that the free trade arrangement in fisheries is good, that the export of our raw, unprocessed salmon and herring on the West Coast, which will also undoubtedly happen on the East Coast, will be an excellent thing. The GATT ruling is protected in the free trade agreement-or the Mulroney free trade agreement, and there is nothing free about this. We will pay through the nose until hell freezes over.
The Minister of Transport is actually advocating that as a valuable thing that has been protected under the trade agreement with the United States. On the other hand, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans states that it is absolutely wrong, British Columbians will not lose one job.
The second question here is, who is in charge? The Minister of Transport speaking on fisheries today, attempting to give this country a snow job on free trade, or the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans standing up and advocating that that GATT arrangement should not go through, that it should not be honoured and that the raw product in British Columbia and Atlantic Canada should be processed in this country?
The third point on which 1 would like a response is the desperation technique of attempting to fan the fire of regional racism in this country. I am not sure whether he did this in his usual exercise of an incredible sense of humour, or whether he put this before the House through his lack of intellect, but the Minister knows that the auto trade is a managed trade agreement in a specific sector. It was carefully thought out and worked out. There were bugs in it when it came through, and people pointed out those bugs, but it was a managed trade agreement in a sector that was worked out very thoroughly before it went into place, and it has derived benefits for Canadians. What the Government did was to put forward an agreement, a proposal to sell this country out. That is not a free trade agreement, and the Minister of Transport knows it. This country will lose its sovereignty. It will pay through the nose forever, if this agreement goes through.

Mr. Speaker, that is about the weakest, most insipid, and most dishonest series of remarks that I have heard in the House in a long time.
1 just finished explaining how the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister for International Trade were taking this GATT panel decision to which we are subject because we are members of GATT, and because we have to trade to live, therefore, we have to be members of GATT which is an organization that both opposition Parties support, and those Ministers were going to appeal it and do everything that is possible to resolve the issue in our favour, or to see that processing of unprocessed fish still continues to be processed in Canada. The hon. gentleman ended up talking about sovereignty. That sovereignty argument is not going to wash.
The European common market and the countries that make it up have gone far further than a free trade arrangement. Yet, is anyone suggesting that any one of those countries has lost its sovereignty? They have not lost their sovereignty. They have entered into a whole common market. The labour movements in those countries opposed it. They had the same short-sighted approach. You are the most reactionary body in society today. You oppose everything that is a change in the status quo. You are just selfish and want to hold on to what you conceive are your own gains; small-minded and inward looking.
By entering the European common market has England lost its sovereignty? Has Mrs. Thatcher lost her sovereignty? Has she lost the power to control her destiny? Has France lost its sovereignty? Has a small country like Belgium lost its sovereignty? Has Luxembourg lost its sovereignty? Of course they have not lost their sovereignty. They have not even lost their what-do-you-call-it-virginity. Somebody says that they have not even lost their virginity.
Yet we are supposed to accept this as a serious argument against a free trade arrangement that Canada is losing its sovereignty. The only way that we can retain our sovereignty is if we retain our capacity to grow and increase our economic strength. That is what gives a country sovereignty. What good is sovereignty to Canada if we have a shrinking market and a declining standard of living?
A month or two ago Doug Fisher pointed out in his column that in the 1960s Mr. Pearson's Government looked at the question of what we could do if we took the protectionist role and got out of our international GATT obligations or ceased any attempt to co-operate with the U.S. How would we survive on our own? The conclusion of the study was that there would be a decline of our standard of living of 25 per cent. The Government wisely concluded that no one in Canada would take that route and willingly forgo 25 per cent of their standard of living to follow the route that is now advocated by the so-called Canadian nationalists.
We know, of course, that the Leader of the Opposition would not take that route either because he is for free trade, and he is against free trade, but he is more for free trade than against free trade. Although he is not for this free trade agreement, he is for some other free trade agreement that he thinks that he could get that nobody else could get. Well, it is no wonder that he did not get anything when he was in for two or three months. He was too busy appointing people to the livestock feed board where they are still feeding away.

Of course, irrespective of inflation, as suggested by my colleague the Hon. Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), which means that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is now operating with a lot less money than in 1984 and 1985. This simply does not make sense.
Mr. Speaker, we could review the way the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has tried-and now I am using their own words-to improve a number of programs especially designed for fishermen. I am referring here to the Fishing Vessel Insurance Plan which was tailored to the needs of fishermen and made it possible for them to obtain lower insurance premium rates.
Because of certain changes which were made to improve this program, the rates are now much higher and the fishermen no longer find the program attractive. They are forced to get their insurance elsewhere because the Government has decided that it would no longer help them with their insurance. Some will say: "Well, why not?" A program was developed and implemented by and for the fishermen. What reasons could there be to say that the program was not worth much and could simply be cancelled? Yet, this is exactly what happened. Conditions were brought in which the fishermen found unacceptable and the program is no longer attractive.
Then, there is the boat-building subsidy program. Mr. Speaker, in the regions of this country where there are fishermen, you only have to mention the boat subsidy program and everyone will know what you are talking about. Fishermen could have a $50,000, $60,000 or $100,000 boat built for inshore fishing, or a bigger boat costing much more money, but in my region, it was mostly $50,000 to $60,000, and they
could obtain a subsidy to help them build it. Fishermen finally could afford the boats which they needed and which had the safety features necessary to give them peace of mind. What happened to that program? Mr. Speaker, this is a very good example of how this Government has given in to the Americans. The Americans said: "Your boat-building program subsidizes the fishing industry and we shall therefore apply countervailing duties." When the minister heard what the Americans were planning, he said: "No, do not do that, we shall simply remove the program completely."
This is exactly what he did. The fishermen can no longer benefit from this program which helped them build their boats for so many years. The Government simply and remorselessly cancelled the program. This is how the Government reacted to the threatened intervention by the Americans, by simply giving in.
There is a lot of talk about free trade. Ministers are travelling throughout Canada saying that free trade-we should perhaps call it the Mulroney treaty with the United States-is the magical solution and what the fishing industry had been waiting for. Now, we have no more reason to worry about our fishing industry. All the problems have been solved. However, when we ask how this industry will benefit from the agreement, we find it difficult to get answers.
We hear from the fishermen's association that they are somehow happy with the free trade deal, but when we ask them why, we get the answer that we have enhanced status quo.

What is the meaning of enhanced status quo?

There you are. My colleague had the answer.
Mr. Speaker, it means that this agreement, this Mulroney treaty, does not mean anything at all in terms of fisheries, it simply has no positive impact in the fishing sector. And when we are told about the agreement provisions concerning trade dispute settlement, and we are told that this mechanism will solve all our problems, we look at the fine print of these provisions and come to the conclusion that this mechanism does not entail any kind of power. In cases where countervailing duties have been imposed, they will quite simply examine the situation to find out whether the duties were imposed pursuant to American legislation, whether they are in accordance with American laws. And if they are, Mr. Speaker, nothing will change as was the case with respect to soft lumber, potash, and shingles. There is no way this mechanism will serve Canadian interests.
November 20, 1987

And yet they keep telling people, fishermen particularly, that the provisions of the agreement are just what they wanted. That settles all problems. We are also told that we are gaining access to the American market. Of course we have access to the American market. We have always sold to the Americans, especially in the Atlantic regions. So what more do we get out of this? Well, absolutely nothing. We quite simply have the same access. Someone might have asked what kind of protection the fishing industry could have under the agreement. Well, we can see now that there is absolutely no protection for fishermen or for all interested parties in the fishing sector. There is nothing to prevent the Americans from taking over our first processing companies and plants and, by the same token, from monopolizing some of the fish stocks we want to keep for ourselves. And there is no protection in the Agreement against this kind of takeover.
We could go on discussing the Free Trade Agreement and the Mulroney-U.S. deal at infinitum. However, I would rather talk about the Small Craft Harbours Program that was discussed with considerable verve yesterday morning. We were told that at last we had a program that would solve all the problems of our fishermen. There would be harbours for small boats, wharves would be repaired, channels would be dredged, and all other problems related to fisheries would be taken care of. Of course everyone welcomed the funds that had been allocated. I did so myself. However, Mr. Speaker, in recent years, we saw a reduction in fund, for repairing small craft harbours. Wharves could no longer be repaired and in some cases had to be barricaded. People were advised not to go to certain areas because it was dangerous to do so. Access channels to the wharves could no longer be dredged. In some cases, fishermen had trouble leaving the wharf to go fishing and had to watch the tides.
And this despite the fact that where I come from, fishing vessels don't draw that much water, not more than one meter or three or four feet. And even there, fishermen were having trouble going out.
Mr. Speaker, you must realize that in my part of the country, along the Northumberland Strait, we have some very specific problems owing to the fact that storms cause the sand that is carried by the currents to shift and fill up the access channels to the wharves, and these channels have to be dredged every year, or at least often enough to make sure they are open.
As I was saying, the funds to carry out this work had been reduced, and now all of a sudden, they seem to have found the money to do it. Of course they had to find the money, because if they had let the situation continue, some of our wharves would have been lost altogether.
It was high time money was found, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the same funding will continue, so that our harbour facilities will meet the needs of our fisheries.
The creation of harbour authorities was also discussed. These would be set up along the coast and, in fact, would be

committees that would take care of the facilities, make sure someone looks after the lights on the wharves, does minor repairs, and watches the buildings where the bait is stored. Of course we have to have people to do these odd jobs.
But in addition to managing the facilities, they also want to make these authorities responsible for imposing certain fees on users. All 1 can say, Mr. Speaker, is that if the Department of Fisheries and Oceans tries to impose user fees on our fishermen, something is going to give!
I would really like to stand at the end of the dock when the person in charge of collecting these charges will ask the fishermen to pay up. I would really like to be there!
If possible, Mr. Speaker, I would like the Minister of Fisheries to ask the Minister of Transport himself to go to the end of the docks to collect these charges from the fishermen. That would be amusing, much more amusing than what we saw this afternoon because our fishermen will simply not accept these user charges.
The Government is trying to do by the back door what it was unable to do by the front door in Bill C-75. We debated that Bill at length, to such an extent that the Hon. Member for Humber-Port-au-Port-Sainte-Barbe (Mr. Tobin) spoke for nearly seven hours to block it. Section 4 of the Bill would have applied the user pay principle.
The Bill did not receive passage, but the Department of Fisheries now has a plan to impose user charges anyway. I really do not see how the Department can collect these charges.
I would like to take this opportunity to speak about a major project which will probably go forward because this is not the first time we hear about it. I am talking about the fixed or dry link between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
If a bridge, or even a tunnel is built, because it might be one or the other, it will have to go through some of the best fishing grounds in New Brunswick. In the Northumberland Strait between Cape Tormentine and Borden on Prince Edward Island, you go through a fishing zone which produces a rich lobster harvest. Indeed, these last few years, this has been the highest yielding sector for lobster fishermen.
Mr. Speaker, the fishermen were told that they would be consulted and that all the studies on the environmental impact and the effects on fishing would be made available. A few meetings were held in New Brunswick. The first steps were taken, but after the studies were completed, Public Works officials did not go back to consult the fishermen.
Now I mention this, Mr. Speaker, because I want to make sure that the Minister of Fisheries will accept responsibility for defending the interests of Northumberland Strait fishermen, because if this bridge or tunnel project were to have a negative impact on fishing, that might prove to be a disaster for all

November 20, 1987
Supply
people in my riding. Indeed, not only fishermen depend on fishing, but so do all lobster processing plant workers.
We heard recently that the project would have no impact on fishing. Well, Mr. Speaker, I fail to see how anyone can make that kind of statement. If they are going to build a bridge to cross over to Prince Edward Island, it certainly will not be a suspension bridge spanning the full width of the strait. They will have to build foundations, piers resting on the bottom of the strait, they will have to dig, they will have to dredge. And if they disturb the bottom, they will certainly disturb the habitat of the lobster and that of scallops, for there are also lots of scallops in that region.
I mention this this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, because I want to make sure that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) will assume responsibility for seeing to it that this project will not have a negative impact on fishing. And should the project indeed have such a negative impact, either during or after the construction phase, the Minister will have to set up a mechanism at the earliest opportunity, that is before work begins, a mechanism to provide compensation for fishermen who will be affected by the bridge or tunnel construction project.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question and a comment. I want to thank the Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud) for a very good speech. He is an excellent Member of the House of Commons and he certainly represents his riding and the interests of the people in Westmorland-Kent and New Brunswick very well.
It was refreshing to hear a sincere and honest speech in the House today on this most important motion put forward by myself and seconded by the Hon. Member compared to the outburst, if you will, by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) who tried to liken this Mulroney-Reagan trade fiasco to the European Economic Community and the trade deal within the EEC. The Minister drew the analogy that we could not live within our own borders. He said that we could not live simply within our own borders. No one disagrees with that. Members of the Opposition are not saying that we should only trade within our own country. Our Party has always stood for multilateral trade, trade with all different countries, and for trade that is enhanced in every way. However, we are now talking about a deal that left far too much out.
The Minister of Transport tried to give the House the impression that we stood only for trade within our own borders. Obviously this is the story government Members are carrying across the country. It is simply not true.
The Minister said: "You wash my socks and I will wash your shirts". That analogy is incorrect because one cannot liken Canada and the United States to the European Economic Community. There are many millions of people in the European Economic Community. We in Canada live alongside a
giant. There are 260 million people in the United States, whereas there are 25 million people in Canada.
Under this deal, which offers no protection whatsoever for most of our natural resource industries, we will be pressing the pants of the people in Washington. As well, we will be washing their dirty underwear. That is the analogy I would draw.
I would like to deal with a few of the issues mentioned by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent. One such issue was the harbour authorities which are being put in place by the Government. Yesterday, we dealt for a couple of hours with concurrence on a motion for increased funding for small craft harbours. We all agree with that, but does the Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent believe that the harbour authorities that are now being appointed are simply a backdoor approach to collecting more revenues at harbours and ports? In other words, is the Government trying to get the fishermen themselves to levy user fees on themselves rather than following through with the Government's original intent which was to have the Government itself do it?
I would also like to comment on the P.E.I. crossing. The Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent and I agree in general principle with a fixed crossing bridge or tunnel to Prince Edward Island. My concern and the concern of the Hon. Member, on which he may comment, surrounds the environmental aspects of the project. It is very important that there be no adverse environmental effects if such a structure is to be built across the Northumberland Strait.
If the fishery is adversely affected in any way, there must be a mechanism put in place before construction of such a crossing or facility is begun. The fishermen should know right from the start that if there are to be adverse effects, some meaningful compensation would be paid to them for the duration of the construction of the structure if it happened to be a bridge. If a bridge were to be built, the pilings and foundation work would obviously disrupt somewhat the lobster and scallop grounds in those areas during construction, and that would take away some of the income of the fishermen. Perhaps the Hon. Member could comment on that issue as well. Perhaps he could tell us whether or not he agrees with me that we are in agreement with the general principle of this, provided that those two important items are looked after along with a number of other items.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FISHERIES-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT MISMANAGEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also thank my colleague the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) for his comments and questions. I should like to mention here the contribution of my colleague on the Fisheries and Oceans Committee who, throughout the Committee proceedings, has forced the Minister to look into the harbour facility situation and make sure that enough money would be available to carry out the necessary repair work. I commend him, therefore, for his efforts which seem to have been successful.
November 20, 1987

As to the port authorities, 1 do believe that, afraid to go directly to the fishermen and ask for users' fees, the Government will try to do it through a committee. I feel it is not quite right for the Minister to tell fishermen to get together and devise development plans for the facilities, in order to be the first to get the funds appropriated for small craft harbour repairs.
Fishermen will then be faced with a dilemma: on the one hand, if they refuse to get organized, they will not be able to get Government's funds to repair their facilities; if, on the other hand, they get organized, they will be the first to obtain part of this money. 1 suggest it is not quite straightforward to operate in that way.
Concerning a fixed link, either a bridge or a tunnel, I agree with my colleague the Flon. Member for Egmont who lives on Prince Edward Island that such a structure should be built provided it has no adverse effect on the fisheries in my area. The Hon. Member also mentioned a compensation mechanism. A precedent exists already. Before the Miramichi River was dredged in the early 1980s, a mechanism had been put in place to compensate the affected fishermen, and 1 can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this way to operate was quite successful in the sense that a number of fishermen were appointed to sit on this committee, together with representatives of Public Works Canada and the contractor doing the work. Mr. Speaker, I should like such a mechanism to be put in place before construction work starts either on a bridge or a tunnel.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FISHERIES-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT MISMANAGEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the greatest of respect for and, I believe, friendship with the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson). We have got along well over the last eight years. I am very disappointed in the motion he brought forward today. It will not impinge upon our friendship or upon my respect for the gentleman, but it does put into question his judgment and his knowledge of the industry we are discussing today.
I had a great 20-minute speech planned but I only have 10 minutes left. Therefore, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak for a moment before I deal with the GATT panel about what the free trade agreement will do for the fisheries. We have heard a lot of scare tactics, so I would like to put on the record of the House of Commons the facts regarding the free trade agreement and fishermen.
The free trade agreement which has been negotiated between the United States and Canada is a tremendous deal for the fishermen and for the fish processors. It is going to bring down tariff barriers to our exports. It is going to protect our fish products from vexatious countervail and anti-dumping actions, and reduce technical barriers which have hampered our exports. Those technical barriers are better known as nontariff barriers.
Supply
Canada's export of fish products to the U.S. totalled almost $1.5 billion in 1986, almost one-third of which were subject to duty. Elimination of those tariffs will particularly benefit processors of fresh and frozen groundfish fillets, prepared fish products such as fish sticks, which are currently facing a U.S. tariff of from 10 per cent to 17.5 per cent. That tariff will disappear with the free trade agreement. Do they mean to say that will not help our fishermen? It will not help our fish processors? How can they stand up here all day long and say it will not help?
Those products I mentioned, including crab meat, represent over 90 per cent of dutiable Canadian fish trade with the U.S. The tariffs on fresh frozen fish, fish-meal, and anchovies- which, I must say, I am not a fan of, even though I know the Minister is-will be lifted as soon as the agreement goes into effect. Reductions will begin on all other tariff items. By January 1, 1994, U.S. tariffs will have been eliminated on fish fillets, salmon, mackerel, clams and, guess what, lobster.
To give an indication of what this means in concrete terms, exports in 1986 to the U.S of lobster from New Brunswick totalled $84 million. From Nova Scotia it was $97 million. Newfoundland's export of fresh and frozen fillets to the U.S. were valued at $331 million last year. British Columbia exported $50 million worth of salmon and salmon products. All other fish products, including tuna, fish sticks, prepared meals, herring, crab, and others will be duty-free by January 1, 1989. These products will gain market share through elimination of tariff barriers. Growing and more secure markets will lead to more processing taking place in Canada and more jobs for Canadians.
Industry spokesmen, the people who put their money on the line to create the plants and hire the people, all say this will be good for their industry. We hear opposition politicians running around this country like Chicken Little saying the sky is falling. Yet Canadian entrepreneurs, the people who take the risk, are saying this is great.
I watched the great debate the CBC had on trade last night between the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) and the Hon. Minister of State for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs (Mrs. McDougall). Do you know who the most excited people were? The young people. They love it. One of them was from Windsor and he said, "You mean I can't compete with those guys across the border in Detroit? You're crazy. I can compete with them." The young people are excited about this deal.
Then we have Ron Bulmer, President of the Fisheries Council of Canada, who said that we will be getting better access to a market of 250 million people for our processed products. These are the guys who can make it happen. They are not afraid of it. They are looking forward to it. They want it. As a matter of fact, they are the ones who encouraged us to get into these negotiations. It was industry-driven. We are not afraid of this. The industry is not afraid of this. It is that little

November 20, 1987

red rump over there who want to be isolationist. Stop the world, I want to get off, that is the way they like to operate. That is what they are trying to do when they go through the country scaring people. It is totally unfounded.
I could go on and on and on about the fishery, quoting chapter and verse of what those people involved in the industry are saying about this. It is a great deal for fishermen and fish processors. For my friend to come along and say we have sold out to the Americans, that is just poppycock. Those big bad Americans are going to come up here, oh, dear, and take us over. Canadians are not that gullible. They have not taken us over since this country came into existence and they are not going to do it now.
We are proud Canadians. We are Canadian nationalists. We believe strongly in Canada. For this Captain Canada, Mel Hurtig, to run around the country saying he is a better Canadian than I am or a better Canadian than the Prime Minister (Mr, Mulroney) is fraud. He is a fraud. What total and absolute nonsense. Tariffs have been coming down from an average of 40 per cent to an average of 9 per cent over the last number of years. Have we lost out to the Americans because of it? No, we have gained strength. In that period we have had prosperity, except for that time during the early 1980s when the Liberals were in power. That was a disaster. Do you know why? Because they hog-tied every industry in this country, especially the energy industry, and we do not want to see that happen again ever.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FISHERIES-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT MISMANAGEMENT
speechtext: And Captain Canada supported them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FISHERIES-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT MISMANAGEMENT
speechtext:
That is right. He sure did.
I want to cover briefly the matter of the GATT panel because there have been so many inaccuracies coming out about that. This is the genesis of the issue and this should be understood by Canadians. This action was primarily brought by Alaskan processors. They wanted the same deal for American processors as Canadians had for their processors. In other words, they wanted to make sure that American-caught fish was sold to American processing plants. Our processing plants were buying raw fish from Alaska. The Americans just said they wanted to be treated the same way. The GATT panel kind of twisted this thing around. Instead of saying that American processors should be treated the same way, they said that this was an unfair trade practice. We understand the problems. The Americans understand the problems. We have GATT procedures which we are following and will continue to follow.
The only thing I have time to say is to assure the workers in the industry-the fishermen have a different attitude towards this GATT panel then do the processors-that we are working diligently with the B.C. Government, the unions and the industry to ensure that the results will be beneficial to all concerned. Canada will maintain its reputation as a fair trader and it will continue to be great for the economy of this country.
